  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models <span class="ltx_pubnotes"><span class="ltx_pubnotes_content"><span class="ltx_pubnote ltx_role_thanks"><span class="ltx_note_name">Thanks: </span>Corresponding author.</span></span></span></h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">

<span class="ltx_personname">Chao Zeng
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Songwei Liu
</span><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_note ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>Project Leader.</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Yusheng Xie
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">

Fangmin Chen,

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized natural language processing tasks. However, their practical application is constrained by substantial memory and computational demands. Post-training quantization (PTQ) is considered an effective method to accelerate LLM inference. Despite its growing popularity in LLM model compression, PTQ deployment faces two major challenges. First, low-bit quantization leads to performance degradation. Second, restricted by the limited integer computing unit type on GPUs, quantized matrix operations with different precisions cannot be effectively accelerated. To address these issues, we introduce a novel arbitrary-bit quantization algorithm and inference framework, ABQ-LLM. It achieves superior performance across various quantization settings and enables efficient arbitrary-precision quantized inference on the GPU. ABQ-LLM introduces several key innovations: (1) a distribution correction method for transformer blocks to mitigate distribution differences caused by full quantization of weights and activations, improving performance at low bit-widths. (2) the bit balance strategy to counteract performance degradation from asymmetric distribution issues at very low bit-widths (e.g., 2-bit). (3) an innovative quantization acceleration framework that reconstructs the quantization matrix multiplication of arbitrary precision combinations based on BTC (Binary TensorCore) equivalents, gets rid of the limitations of INT4/INT8 computing units. ABQ-LLM can convert each component bit width gain into actual acceleration gain, maximizing performance under mixed precision(e.g., W6A6, W2A8). Based on W2*A8 quantization configuration on LLaMA-7B model, it achieved a WikiText2 perplexity of 7.59 (2.17<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math> vs 9.76 in AffineQuant). Compared to SmoothQuant, we realized 1.6<math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> acceleration improvement and 2.7<math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> memory compression gain. Code will available at: <span class="ltx_ref ltx_nolink ltx_url ltx_ref_self">https://github.com/bytedance/ABQ-LLM</span>.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="id2" class="ltx_logical-block ltx_align_bottom">
    
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><sup id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_sup"></sup> ByteDance Inc.</p>
<p id="p1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">{zengchaocs, cfangmin}@gmail.com,</p>
<p id="p1.3" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">{liusongwei.zju, xieyusheng.12, liuhong.10, wangxiaojian.wxj, weimiao.brandon, yang.1109, xing.mei}@bytedance.com</p>
</div>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bubeck et al. 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al. 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al. 2023b</a>)</cite> have demonstrated impressive capabilities across various natural language benchmark, including reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Clark et al. 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Clark et al. 2018</a>)</cite>, cognitive processing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al. 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hardy et al. 2023</a>)</cite>, and dialogue generation<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al. 2023</a>)</cite>. However, these models are characterized by a substantial number of parameters, posing significant challenges in terms of memory consumption and bandwidth <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al. 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Post-training quantization (PTQ) effectively reduces both computational and storage requirements. This technique significantly accelerates model inference by converting the weights and activation values of large language models (LLMs) from high-precision floating-point numbers to low-precision integer values for storage, and using efficient integer matrix multiplication operators to handle the bulk of matrix multiplication computations during inference. Currently, 80% of the computation and parameter access in LLMs is concentrated on general matrix multiplication (GEMM) and vector multiplication (GEMV) operations, especially during autoregressive decoding, where all GEMM operations degrade into GEMV operations due to single-token generation. Consequently, the efficiency of GEMV computation and memory access directly determines the efficiency and power consumption of LLM inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To improve GEMM/GEMV memory access efficiency, LLM inference typically employs a quantized inference strategy. The current mainstream approach is weight-only quantization, where the kernel performs actual computation based on dequantized FP16 values. However, this approach offers limited performance improvement in highly parallel scenarios. To further enhance quantized inference performance, the industry is pursuing full quantization of both weights and activation values to reduce activation memory access and leverage higher computational power using quantized kernels, such as those from NVIDIA. However, current industry practices in weight and activation full quantization (WA full quantization) face several limitations. NVIDIA provides only a limited set of hardware-accelerated instructions<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al. 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ashkboos et al. 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al. 2024</a>)</cite>, which constrains the design space for quantization algorithms. Other quantization combinations (e.g., W4A8 or W2A4) require type conversion to W8A8 or W4A4 during computation, leading to inefficiency<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al. 2024b</a>)</cite>. Furthermore, due to GEMV, additional padding calculations are required in scenarios with a batch size less than 8, resulting in inefficient matrix multiplication for W4A4 and W8A8. Finally, WA fully quantized models encounter significant challenges in low-bit quantization (e.g., W2A8, W2A6).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2408.08554v3/wikitext_ppl.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:628/468;" width="628" height="468" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Perplexities analysis (lower is better) on the Wikitext2 dataset of LLaMA-7B with different quantized modules.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we introduce a novel quantization framework for PTQ, called ABQ-LLM. By examining the quantization sensitivity of components within the transformer block (Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) and the attention map before and after quantization (Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), we find the down_proj linear layer and the attention map particularly sensitive to quantization. To address this, we propose a double cosine similarity distribution correction and an attention map distribution bootstrap for the output of down_proj. This method calibrates the quantization constants and restores the model’s performance at low bit-widths such as W6A6, W4A4 and W2A8. Additionally, we analyze performance degradation in low-bit quantization and address the asymmetric loss issue in low-bit representations like INT2 using the bit balance strategy. Finally, we implement customized software engine to support fully quantized inference of various precision combinations based on BTC equivalents, fully exploiting the advantages
of quantized models under mixed precision. Our contributions are summarized as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose a novel block-wise distribution correction and compensation scheme in the PTQ domain to mitigate the distribution discrepancy caused by full quantization of weights and activations, thereby improving model performance at low bit-widths.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We address the problem of asymmetric loss at low bit-widths, such as INT2, and significantly improve INT2 quantization performance using the bit balance strategy, enhancing model performance under the INT2 quantization configuration.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose a software engine which achieves quantization freedom for the first time in the LLM field. It eliminates the limitations of INT4/INT8 computational units, and effectively avoids the GEMV problem. Under the LLaMA-7B W2A8 configuration, it has 1.6<math id="S1.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> ultimate acceleration compared to SmoothQuant, achieving SOTA performance.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2408.08554v3/attention_map.png" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:698/499;" width="698" height="499" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Attention maps for the first block (above) and the final block (below) are shown.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">LLM quantization can be broadly divided into weight-only quantization and weight-activation quantization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Weight-only quantization.</span> To alleviate computational burdens, some studies focus on weight-only quantization. LLM.int8() <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dettmers et al. 2022</a>)</cite> achieves accurate INT8 quantization by retaining significant channels. GPTQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Frantar et al. 2022</a>)</cite> uses Hessian-based error compensation to reduce quantization errors in LLMs, enabling 3-bit quantization. AWQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al. 2024a</a>)</cite> and OWQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al. 2024</a>)</cite> significantly enhance quantized model performance by considering the impact of activation outliers on weight quantization. Methods like QuIP<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chee et al. 2024</a>)</cite>, QuIP# <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tseng et al. 2024</a>)</cite>, and AQLM<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Egiazarian et al. 2024</a>)</cite> facilitate 2-bit quantization through learnable codebooks or additional fine-tuning. Approaches such as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dettmers et al. 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shang et al. 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al. 2024</a>)</cite> improve PTQ performance through unstructured mixed-precision fine-grained weight grouping. Additionally, research such as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dettmers et al. 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al. 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arshia et al. 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bondarenko, Del Chiaro, and Nagel 2024</a>)</cite> employs efficient parameter fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques to compress weights through fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Weight-activation quantization.</span> Weight-activation quantization differs from weight-only quantization by quantizing both weights and activation (including KV caches) to accelerate LLM inference. The main challenge in quantizing activation is handling outliers, which can cause significant quantization errors. To address this issue, ZeroQuant<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al. 2022</a>)</cite> proposes a fine-grained, hardware-friendly quantization scheme for weights and activation. SmoothQuant<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al. 2023</a>)</cite> shifts the quantization difficulty from activation to weights through mathematically equivalent transformations, achieving W8A8 quantization. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al. 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al. 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al. 2024a</a>)</cite> enhances performance by training quantization parameters. Limited by GPU platform instruction limitations, these jobs can only use W8A8 to perform actual inference, even if they achieve lower quantization bit-widths (e.g., W6A6).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we provide a detailed introduction to our ABQ-LLM. We first describe the distribution correction and bit balance strategy and then introduce our arbitrary-bit inference framework.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2408.08554v3/ABQ-LLM.png" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:698/388;" width="698" height="388" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>An overview of our ABQ-LLM. ABQ-LLM use our DLC loss and AKL loss to update learnable parameters.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Preliminary</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al. 2023</a>)</cite> achieves WA full quantization by scaling activation outliers, but this increases the range variability of weights, making weight quantization more sensitive. Conversely, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al. 2024a</a>)</cite> optimizes weight quantization by scaling weights, which significantly increases the diversity of activation, complicating activation quantization. These approaches highlight the drawbacks of manually setting scaling balance factors between activation and weight, making it challenging to achieve a perfect balance. To address this issue, we introduce a distribution correction-guided scaling method. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al. 2023</a>)</cite> approach, we set the balance vectors between weights and activation as learnable parameters and add a learnable clipping parameter for weight. By employing our distribution correction and bit balance strategy to optimize model performance, our objectives are as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E1X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E1X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\scalebox{0.9}{$\underset{s,\alpha,\beta}{\text{argmin}}\left\|WX-Q(\text{clip}(W)\cdot\text{diag}(s))Q(\text{diag}(s)^{-1}\cdot X)\right\|,$}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mpadded style="width:221.2pt;height:9.6pt;vertical-align:-2.3pt;" depth="2.3pt" height="7.3pt" width="221.2pt"><mrow><munder accentunder="true"><mtext>argmin</mtext><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em">s</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">α</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">β</mi></mrow></munder><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mtext>clip</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>W</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mtext>diag</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext>diag</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mpadded><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\scalebox{0.9}{$\underset{s,\alpha,\beta}{\text{argmin}}\left\|WX-Q(\text{clip}(W)\cdot\text{diag}(s))Q(\text{diag}(s)^{-1}\cdot X)\right\|,$}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> are full-precision weight and activation, <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the quantizer of weight and activation, <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{clip}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>clip</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{clip}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the clipping operation, <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> is the scale factor, and letting <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{max}=\alpha\text{max}(W)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" encoding="application/x-tex">W_{max}=\alpha\text{max}(W)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{min}=\beta\text{min}(W)" display="inline" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>min</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{min}=\beta\text{min}(W)</annotation></semantics></math> to control the clipping range of the weight.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Improving Quantization by Distribution Correction</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">We observed significant variations in sensitivity across different layers of LLM models during quantization, with some layers having a critical impact on quantization performance. To validate this, as shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we quantified various components of the LLaMA-7B model under weight-activation full quantization. While quantizing the gate_proj and up_proj layers in mlp and attention resulted in only minor performance degradation, quantizing the down_proj linear layer caused a substantial performance drop. This indicates that addressing down_proj quantization is crucial for performance recovery. Further analysis revealed that the primary cause of performance degradation due to down_proj quantization is the quantization of down_proj activation. At low bit-widths such as INT4, INT3, and INT2, the limited representation range causes a significant shift in the model distribution compared to full precision. As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3 Method ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, during the block-wise quantization calibration process, we apply a <span id="S3.SS2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">d</span>ouble <span id="S3.SS2.p1.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">l</span>ogarithm of <span id="S3.SS2.p1.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">c</span>osine similarity loss on the output of down_proj to correct the distribution of the quantized model. The loss function called DLC loss <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}^{i}_{DLC}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}^{i}_{DLC}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E2X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{i}_{DLC}=-\text{log}(\frac{d^{i}_{q}\cdot rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>‖</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" d^{i}_{fp^{*}}}{\left\|d^{i}_{q}\right\|\left\|d^{i}_{fp^{*}}\right\|}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d^{i}_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d^{i}_{q}</annotation></semantics></math> represent the quantized output of the <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th transformer block, <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d^{i}_{fp}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d^{i}_{fp}</annotation></semantics></math> represent the full-precision output of the <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th transformer block, and <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d^{i}_{fp^{*}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>p</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d^{i}_{fp^{*}}</annotation></semantics></math> represent the full-precision output of the <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th transformer block, with its input originating from the quantized output of the <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(i-1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(i-1)</annotation></semantics></math>-th transformer block.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Additionally, we conducted an analysis of the cosine similarity between activation at the input and output of decoder blocks in the LLaMA-7B model. The results revealed significant differences in similarity for the initial and final blocks, indicating their considerable impact on model inference performance. In response, we applied distribution compensation vector to the down_proj layers of these blocks to address and correct the distribution discrepancies using Eq. (<a href="#S3.E3" title="In 3.2 Improving Quantization by Distribution Correction ‣ 3 Method ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E3X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E3X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle W_{q}=\text{clamp}(\lceil\frac{W+\gamma ab^{\top}}{\bigtriangleup}\rfloor+z,0,2^{n}-1)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>clamp</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌈</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>△</mo></mfrac></mstyle><mo stretchy="false">⌋</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle W_{q}=\text{clamp}(\lceil\frac{W+\gamma ab^{\top}}{\bigtriangleup}\rfloor+z,0,2^{n}-1),</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lceil\cdot\rfloor" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌈</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">⌋</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lceil\cdot\rfloor</annotation></semantics></math> denotes round operation, <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> represents the target bit-width, <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bigtriangleup" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>△</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bigtriangleup</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the step-size, and <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> is the zero-point. <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{q}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> denote the quantized and full-presicion weight, respectively. The vectors <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> are distribution compensation vectors, where <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma=1</annotation></semantics></math> indicates compensation is performed, and <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma=0</annotation></semantics></math> indicates no compensation.</p>
</div>

<span id="S3.F4.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">p</span> and <span id="S3.F4.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">q</span> represent the quantization bit width of input X and weight W. Data flows are carefully designed to support efficient computation: global memory(<span id="S3.F4.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GL</span>) <math id="S3.F4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> shared memory(<span id="S3.F4.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SMEM</span>) <math id="S3.F4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> fragment(<span id="S3.F4.15" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">FR</span>) <math id="S3.F4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> shared memory(<span id="S3.F4.16" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SMEM</span>) <math id="S3.F4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> global memory(<span id="S3.F4.17" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GL</span>). (b) ABQ-LLM’s calculation diagram for a Transformer block. <span id="S3.F4.18" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ReQuant</span> and <span id="S3.F4.19" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DeQuant</span> represent online quantization and dequantization operations respectively, and <span id="S3.F4.20" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">BitPacking</span> represents the online layout transformation for activation.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.2" class="ltx_p">To enhance the performance of the quantized model, we analyzed the changes in Attention Map distribution before and after quantization, as shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. In the full-precision model, attention is heavily focused on the first token, highlighting its key role in guiding text generation, consistent with LLM-QAT<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. 2023</a>)</cite> findings. However, quantization disrupts this attention pattern, diminishing focus on the first token. To address this and restore the model’s attention during quantization, we introduced <span id="S3.SS2.p4.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">a</span>ttention-aware <span id="S3.SS2.p4.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">KL</span> divergence to reconstruct the attention map.</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E4X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\scalebox{0.9}{$\mathcal{L}^{i}_{AKL}=D_{KL}(attn^{i}_{q}\parallel attn^{i}_{fp})+D_{KL}(attn^{i}_{fp}\parallel attn^{i}_{q}),$}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mpadded style="width:203.4pt;height:10pt;vertical-align:-2.6pt;" depth="2.6pt" height="7.4pt" width="203.4pt"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msup><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>n</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msup><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>n</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msup><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>D</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>n</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msup><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>n</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msup><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>q</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></mpadded><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\scalebox{0.9}{$\mathcal{L}^{i}_{AKL}=D_{KL}(attn^{i}_{q}\parallel attn^{i}_{fp})+D_{KL}(attn^{i}_{fp}\parallel attn^{i}_{q}),$}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="attn^{i}_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">attn^{i}_{q}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the quantized attention map output of the <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th transformer block, while <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="attn^{i}_{fp}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">attn^{i}_{fp}</annotation></semantics></math> refers to the full-precision attention map output of the same block.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.2" class="ltx_p">In the end, we combined DLC loss and AKL loss, and our final optimization goal is:</p>

<tbody>

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E5X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle s^{i}_{*},\alpha^{i}_{*},\beta^{*}_{i}=\underset{s^{i},\alpha^{i},\beta^{i}}{\text{argmin}}(\mathcal{L}^{i}_{DLC}+\mathcal{L}^{i}_{AKL})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mo>∗</mo><mi>i</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mo>∗</mo><mi>i</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>β</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder accentunder="true"><mtext>argmin</mtext><mrow><msup><mi mathsize="0.700em">s</mi><mi mathsize="0.710em">i</mi></msup><mo mathsize="0.700em">,</mo><msup><mi mathsize="0.700em">α</mi><mi mathsize="0.710em">i</mi></msup><mo mathsize="0.700em">,</mo><msup><mi mathsize="0.700em">β</mi><mi mathsize="0.710em">i</mi></msup></mrow></munder><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle s^{i}_{*},\alpha^{i}_{*},\beta^{*}_{i}=\underset{s^{i},\alpha^{i},\beta^{i}}{\text{argmin}}(\mathcal{L}^{i}_{DLC}+\mathcal{L}^{i}_{AKL}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{i}_{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mo>∗</mo><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{i}_{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{i}_{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mo>∗</mo><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha^{i}_{*}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>β</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta^{*}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are the parameters of the <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th transformer block after calibration. When the distributions of the quantized output and the full-precision output match, we have a loss close to 0, which effectively guides the quantization process.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Bit Balance Strategy</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Typically, pre-trained LLM model weight exhibit near-normal distribution, characterized by symmetry. Using Q-Q plots (Quantile-Quantile Plots), we confirmed the strong symmetry in the weight distribution of pre-trained models (see Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Bit Balance Analyze ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>). However, in standard INT2 quantization, the numerical representation is limited to four values, with symmetric quantization ranges of {-2, -1, 0, 1} or {-1, 0, 1, 2}, disrupting the original symmetric weight distribution (see Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Bit Balance Analyze ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>). This asymmetry leads to significant performance degradation, as shown in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.4 Custom Software Engine ‣ 3 Method ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, where performance drops by 0.46 from W4A16 to W3A16 and by 5.19 from W3A16 to W2A16, indicating a sharp decline. To address this asymmetry impact on LLM quantization, we adopted the bit balance strategy like <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al. 2024a</a>)</cite>, extending the INT2 symmetric quantization space to {-2, -1, 0, 1, 2}. This modification restored model performance to 7.50, which is within a reasonable range compared to W3A16.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Custom Software Engine</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reconstructing Arbitrary Bit Computation.</span> To support W1A1 quantization, NVIDIA introduced INT1 TensorCore in Turing and later architectures to provide hardware support. However, W1A1 quantization has not been widely applied due to significant performance degradation. Through mathematical analysis of quantized matrix multiplication, we find that any combination of quantization can be decomposed into a superposition of 1-bit matrix multiplications. Assuming the weight <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> of a particular neural network layer are quantized to <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">q</span> bits and the input activation value <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> is quantized to <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">p</span> bits, the matrix multiplication of <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> results in a 32-bit output <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y=WX" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y=WX</annotation></semantics></math>. The key is to observe that the scalar values at any position in W and X can be decomposed into a series of 1-bit scalar numbers. Scalar operations with any combination of precision can be decomposed into 1-bit operations and shift operations. For example, a 2-bit x can be expressed as:</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E6X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E6X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle x=x^{1}x^{0},\text{where}\quad x^{i}\in\text{INT1}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>where</mtext><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><mo>∈</mo><mtext>INT1</mtext></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle x=x^{1}x^{0},\text{where}\quad x^{i}\in\text{INT1},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{1}=(x\gg 1)\&amp;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≫</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">&amp;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{1}=(x\gg 1)\&amp;1</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{0}=(x\gg 0)\&amp;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≫</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">&amp;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{0}=(x\gg 0)\&amp;1</annotation></semantics></math>. We use <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="OP(a,b)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">OP(a,b)</annotation></semantics></math> to denote a computational operation where the input is 1-bit data and the output is 32-bit. Thus, the original scalar-level arbitrary precision computation <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="wx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">wx</annotation></semantics></math> can be represented as:</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E7X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E7X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle wx=w*(x^{1}x^{0})=OP(w,x^{1})*2+OP(w,x^{0})." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle wx=w*(x^{1}x^{0})=OP(w,x^{1})*2+OP(w,x^{0}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The above procedure can be generalized to any combination of matrix multiplications with bit-widths <span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">p</span> and <span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">q</span>. The detailed formulas are shown in the Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Arbitrary Bit Matrix Calculation ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>. Using these transformations, we decompose the operation of arbitrary quantized combinations into a superposition of 1-bit matrix multiplications, enabling the underlying layer to invoke high-computing instruction implementations.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Performance comparison of LLaMA-7B under W4, W3, and W2 quantization configurations. * denotes the use of the bit balance strategy.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Engine Implementation.</span> NVIDIA GPU has many processing elements called Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) and uses a large number of threads to perform computing tasks in parallel. Threads are structured into thread blocks, which become the smallest scheduling execution unit on SMs. Therefore, the computation target is decomposed and mapped to each thread block, called
<span id="S3.SS4.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Thread Block Tile</span>, to achieve parallel computing. As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.2 Improving Quantization by Distribution Correction ‣ 3 Method ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>(a), for a GEMM task of shape M×N×K, each thread block is responsible for computing a BM×BN output block, which is decomposed into <math id="S3.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{K}{BK}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{K}{BK}</annotation></semantics></math> sub-GEMM tasks of shape BM×BN×BK. Our engine converts quantized matrix multiplications with bit widths configured as {p, q} into special accumulations of p*q binarized matrix multiplications, so the true calculation task of thread block tile is p*BM × q*BN. <span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.SS4.p3.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="15.74" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.41px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.74 15.74" width="15.74"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,15.74) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.87,0) translate(0,7.87)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000"><path d="M 7.59 0 C 7.59 4.19 4.19 7.59 0 7.59 C -4.19 7.59 -7.59 4.19 -7.59 0 C -7.59 -4.19 -4.19 -7.59 0 -7.59 C 4.19 -7.59 7.59 -4.19 7.59 0 Z M 0 0"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#FFFFFF;--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#FFFFFF" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.46 -4.46)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.64em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="8.92" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.92)" width="6.92"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.SS4.p3.pic1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">1</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span> First, in order to improve memory access continuity, we propose <span id="S3.SS4.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">BitPacking</span> strategy to decompose the quantized tensor into <math id="S3.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> binary matrices, where <math id="S3.SS4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> is the quantization bit width. Taking input X as an example, this means that its bit perspective layout changes from [M, K, p] to [p, M, K]. All threads within a thread block share the same shared memory space. Within each thread block, threads are further organized into a set of warps, with each warp consisting of 32 consecutive threads. <span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.SS4.p3.pic2" class="ltx_picture" height="15.74" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.41px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.74 15.74" width="15.74"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,15.74) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.87,0) translate(0,7.87)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000"><path d="M 7.59 0 C 7.59 4.19 4.19 7.59 0 7.59 C -4.19 7.59 -7.59 4.19 -7.59 0 C -7.59 -4.19 -4.19 -7.59 0 -7.59 C 4.19 -7.59 7.59 -4.19 7.59 0 Z M 0 0"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#FFFFFF;--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#FFFFFF" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.46 -4.46)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.64em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="8.92" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.92)" width="6.92"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.SS4.p3.pic2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">2</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span> Next, warps collaborates to load the A matrix (p*BM × BK) and B matrix (BK × q*BN) data required for thread block tile calculation from GL and caches them in SMEM. Thanks to BitPacking, the process of reading p BM*BK single-bit row-major tiles and writing p*BM*BK bits SMEM is efficient and continuous. <span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.SS4.p3.pic3" class="ltx_picture" height="15.74" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.41px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.74 15.74" width="15.74"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,15.74) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.87,0) translate(0,7.87)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000"><path d="M 7.59 0 C 7.59 4.19 4.19 7.59 0 7.59 C -4.19 7.59 -7.59 4.19 -7.59 0 C -7.59 -4.19 -4.19 -7.59 0 -7.59 C 4.19 -7.59 7.59 -4.19 7.59 0 Z M 0 0"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#FFFFFF;--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#FFFFFF" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.46 -4.46)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.64em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="8.92" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.92)" width="6.92"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.SS4.p3.pic3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">3</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span> Subsequently, thread block contains multiple warps, so thread block tile can be further decomposed into <span id="S3.SS4.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Warp Tile</span> to achieve warp-level parallelism, and the computing tasks of each warp are WM× WN. In the calculation preparation stage, the A matrix (WM×WK, row-major) and B matrix (WK×WN, col-major) are independently loaded from SMEM to FR. Then, the calculation is decomposed into WM_TILES*WARP_N_TILES TensorCore MMA(matrix-multiply-accumulate). Since A and B are binarized matrices, we actually use Binary TensorCore MMA (BMMA), which has a computing power 8 times and 4 times higher than INT8 and INT4 TensorCore respectively. <span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.SS4.p3.pic4" class="ltx_picture" height="15.74" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.41px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.74 15.74" width="15.74"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,15.74) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.87,0) translate(0,7.87)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000"><path d="M 7.59 0 C 7.59 4.19 4.19 7.59 0 7.59 C -4.19 7.59 -7.59 4.19 -7.59 0 C -7.59 -4.19 -4.19 -7.59 0 -7.59 C 4.19 -7.59 7.59 -4.19 7.59 0 Z M 0 0"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#FFFFFF;--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#FFFFFF" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.46 -4.46)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.64em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="8.92" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.92)" width="6.92"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.SS4.p3.pic4.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">4</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span> All warps collaboratively complete the Thread Block Tile calculation, and the results are stored in the c fragment of each warp. Therefore, each warp needs to independently write the calculation results back to SMEM. <span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.SS4.p3.pic5" class="ltx_picture" height="15.74" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.41px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.74 15.74" width="15.74"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,15.74) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.87,0) translate(0,7.87)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000"><path d="M 7.59 0 C 7.59 4.19 4.19 7.59 0 7.59 C -4.19 7.59 -7.59 4.19 -7.59 0 C -7.59 -4.19 -4.19 -7.59 0 -7.59 C 4.19 -7.59 7.59 -4.19 7.59 0 Z M 0 0"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#FFFFFF;--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#FFFFFF" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.46 -4.46)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.64em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="8.92" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.92)" width="6.92"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.SS4.p3.pic5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">5</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span> As shown in Eq. (<a href="#A2.E10" title="In Appendix B Arbitrary Bit Matrix Calculation ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>), output tile(p*BM × q*BN) is globally reduced to obtain a final result(BM × BN), where each BM × BN sub-Tile needs to be multiplied by a certain scaling factor. We call this process <span id="S3.SS4.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bit Reduction</span>.
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.SS4.p3.pic6" class="ltx_picture" height="15.74" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.41px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.74 15.74" width="15.74"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,15.74) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.87,0) translate(0,7.87)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000"><path d="M 7.59 0 C 7.59 4.19 4.19 7.59 0 7.59 C -4.19 7.59 -7.59 4.19 -7.59 0 C -7.59 -4.19 -4.19 -7.59 0 -7.59 C 4.19 -7.59 7.59 -4.19 7.59 0 Z M 0 0"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#FFFFFF;--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#FFFFFF" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.46 -4.46)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.64em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="8.92" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.92)" width="6.92"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.SS4.p3.pic6.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">6</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span> As the final step, warps collaboratively load the final result from SMEM and write back to the target location in GL.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We implement the above calculation process as a GPU Kernel, called ABQKernel. As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.2 Improving Quantization by Distribution Correction ‣ 3 Method ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>(b), ABQKernel is used to replace all gemm operations in the decoder layer, and assists with necessary BitPacking, quantization, and dequantization operations to achieve arbitrary quantization inference of the LLaMA model. We carefully manages the overhead of quantization operators by fusing them into existing operators and weight BitPacking is implemented offline for increased efficiency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPU Kernel Optimization.</span> When M=1, the GEMM problem of shape MxNxK transforms into a GEMV problem, shifting from computation-intensive to memory-intensive, which becomes a performance bottleneck for model inference. When using ordinary TensorCore for accelerated computation, the dimensions of M are usually chunked in groups of 8, requiring padding if M<math id="S3.SS4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math>8, leading to 87.5% redundant computation. Thanks to the revolutionary reconstruction of computing and BitPacking strategy, for the <math id="S3.SS4.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{q}A_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{q}A_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> configuration, the actual computing task undertaken by ABQKernel is p*M × q*N × K. The expansion of the M dimension can effectively reduce the redundant calculations when calling TensorCore, and even when p*M <math id="S3.SS4.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mo lspace="0em">⁣</mo><mo>=</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;=</annotation></semantics></math> 8 and p*M <math id="S3.SS4.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>%</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\%</annotation></semantics></math> 8 = 0, padding can be completely avoided. We call the above optimization strategy <span id="S3.SS4.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">GEMV Elimination</span>. In addition, <span id="S3.SS4.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Computational and Pipeline Optimization</span>, <span id="S3.SS4.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> Auto Kernel Search</span>, and <span id="S3.SS4.p5.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Bank Conflicts Elimination</span> are also applied. For details, see Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D GPU Kernel Optimization Details ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<td id="S4.T2.1.12.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">15.70</td>
<td id="S4.T2.1.12.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">26.44</td>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baseline.</span> For weight-only quantization, we compare our approach with GPTQ<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Frantar et al. 2022</a>)</cite>, AWQ<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al. 2024a</a>)</cite>, OmniQuant<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al. 2023</a>)</cite>, and AffineQuant<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al. 2024b</a>)</cite>. For weight-activation quantization, we benchmark our method against SmoothQuant<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al. 2023</a>)</cite>, OmniQuant<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al. 2023</a>)</cite>, and I-LLM<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al. 2024b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Models and Datasets.</span> We primarily evaluate our method using LLaMA (7B-13B) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al. 2023a</a>)</cite> and LLaMA-2 (7B-13B) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al. 2023b</a>)</cite>in this paper. Following previous work<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al. 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al. 2024b</a>)</cite>, we evaluate the quantized models by reporting the perplexity of language generation experiments on WikiText2<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Merity et al. 2016</a>)</cite> and C4<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Raffel et al. 2020</a>)</cite>. To assess performance on zero-shot tasks, we select several popular benchmarks including PIQA<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bisk et al. 2020</a>)</cite>, ARC<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Clark et al. 2018</a>)</cite>, BoolQ<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Clark et al. 2019</a>)</cite>, HellaSwag<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zellers et al. 2019</a>)</cite>, and Winogrande<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sakaguchi et al. 2021</a>)</cite> using the lm-evaluation-harness<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al. 2021</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Calibration</span> We initialize the balance vectors for weights and activations following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al. 2023</a>)</cite>, with the learnable clipping parameter for weights set to 1. For distribution correction compensation vectors, we set <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> as an all-ones vector and <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> as an all-zeros vector, ensuring <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ab^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ab^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math> starts at 0. Using the AdamW optimizer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Loshchilov and Hutter 2017</a>)</cite> with no weight decay, we set learning rates of 5e-3 for balance vectors and 1e-2 for the clipping parameter and vector compensation vector. Calibration data includes 128 randomly selected 2048-token segments from WikiText2. The calibration process, conducted on an NVIDIA A800-40G GPU, utilized a batch size of 1 and spanned 20 epochs. For activation and KV Cache we perform per-token quantization, and for weight we perform per-channel quantization. By default, activation and KV cache use the same quantization bit.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2408.08554v3/speedups.png" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:663/556;" width="663" height="556" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>The GEMV speedup comparison of our ABQKernel, CUTLASS (W4A4/W8A8), and cuBLAS (W8A8) in RTX 3070. The left side is compared against W8A8 and the right side against W4A4.
More result in RTX 4080 can be found in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D GPU Kernel Optimization Details ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> tables <a href="#A4.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ Appendix D GPU Kernel Optimization Details ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>, <a href="#A4.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ Appendix D GPU Kernel Optimization Details ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Experiments on Language Generation Tasks</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Language generation capability is central to large language models (LLMs). To validate our extraordinary performance in the challenging quantization task, we first compare perplexity, a crucial metric for language generation, with the baseline. As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, ABQ-LLM demonstrates outstanding performance across various quantization configurations, surpassing state-of-the-art methods such as AffineQuant and I-LLM. Notably, in the INT2 setting, the application of bit balance strategy yields significant improvements at minimal cost. The W2*A8 configurations substantially outperform the W2A8 configurations. Specifically, perplexity on WikiText2 and C4 datasets decreases by an average of 1.42 and 2.11 points, respectively, for W2*A8 compared to the W4A4. These findings validate the effectiveness of our distribution correction and bit balance strategy. The results of weight-only quantization are presented in Table <a href="#A3.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Appendix C Full Results for Quantization Algorithms ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> at Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Full Results for Quantization Algorithms ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>. Additional results for full WA quantization are provided in Tables <a href="#A3.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Appendix C Full Results for Quantization Algorithms ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> at Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Full Results for Quantization Algorithms ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
