<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Experiments on Zero-Shot Tasks</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To further validate our model, we compare zero-shot accuracy with the baseline method, as shown in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Experiments on Language Generation Tasks ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Our ABQ-LLM method outperforms the previous method in most cases. Notably, after applying the bit balance strategy, the performance of W2*A8 improves significantly by 7.50% on average. Combining the performance in both language generation and zero-shot tasks, we conclude that ABQ-LLM achieves state-of-the-art results in handling challenging quantization tasks. See the Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Full Results for Quantization Algorithms ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> for more results and analysis of quantized configurations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Inference Engine Evaluation</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Kernel Benchmark.</span> We evaluated the GEMV speedup of our ABQKernel across three matrix dimensions in LLaMA-7B and compared it with the quantization kernel provided by cuBLAS and CUTLASS. It is important to note that CUTLASS only supports W4A4 and W8A8, while cuBLAS supports only W8A8 for quantization operations. Our experiments were conducted on two different GPUs: the RTX 4080 and the RTX 3070. Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> presents the results, showing that our ABQKernel achieve superior acceleration across all matrix sizes. Specifically, for special bit combinations such as W2A8 and W2A4, our ABQKernel significantly outperforms the baseline approaches, as cuBLAS and CUTLASS require conversion to W8A8 and W4A4 for computation. In the W2A8 configuration, our throughput is improved by 7.47<math id="S4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> compared to W8A8 with CUTLASS and cuBLAS on dimensions (1, 4096) <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> (4096, 4096).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2408.08554v3/e2e.png" id="S4.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:663/353;" width="663" height="353" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Inference latency (top) and memory usage (bottom) of the FastTransformer implementation on NVIDIA A800-40GB GPU with a fixed input length of 15. More results can be found in at Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D GPU Kernel Optimization Details ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> Table <a href="#A4.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ Appendix D GPU Kernel Optimization Details ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">End-to-end throughput.</span>
As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.4 Inference Engine Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, we integrate our ABQKernel into FastTransformer and compare it with the FP16 implementation of FastTransformer and the INT8 implementation of SmoothQuant. Compared to FP16, our scheme achieves 2.95<math id="S4.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> inference acceleration and 4.8<math id="S4.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> memory compression gain, while requiring only 10GB of memory for inference on the LLaMA-30B model, which is less than the memory required for LLaMA-7B with FP16. Additionally, our scheme achieves 1.6<math id="S4.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup and 2.7<math id="S4.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> memory compression gain over SmoothQuant, significantly outperforming current mainstream inference methods. This substantial improvement reduces the cost of LLM services and facilitates their practical deployment.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Kernel Optimization Ablation.</span> Table 4 presents the impact of various optimization techniques on the inference latency of the kernel when performing the GEMV operation with dimensions (1, 4096) <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> (4096, 4096). Our ABQKernel significantly outperforms the CUTLASS W8A8 kernel when unoptimized. Additionally, by employing pipeline optimization, GEMV elimination and auto kernel search, we achieve a latency reduction by 7.47<math id="S4.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> and a corresponding increase in throughput by 7.47<math id="S4.SS4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>. These results significantly outperform CUTLASS.</p>
</div>

</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present an arbitrary bit quantization inference framework called ABQ-LLM. Through an in-depth analysis of LLM quantization, we introduce distribution correction and bit balance strategy to enhance model performance. We then design a novel arbitrary bit inference engine to fully leverage the advantages of LLM quantization. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that ABQ-LLM achieves outstanding performance across various quantization configurations, including W6A6, W4A4, and W2A8. Moreover, ABQKernel consistently outperformed both CUTLASS and cuBLAS in all configurations. Our end-to-end inference speed is 1.6 <math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster than the industry SOTA, SmoothQuant, and achieves 2.7 <math id="S5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> memory compression gain.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Bit Balance Analyze</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Figure <a href="#A1.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ Appendix A Bit Balance Analyze ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, there is a clear asymmetry in the weights of o_proj after INT2 quantization, particularly evident in the 10th and 20th blocks. This asymmetry shifts the distribution of the model’s weights, resulting in significant performance loss. However, after applying the balancing strategy, the distribution of weights closely aligns with that of the full-precision model, as illustrated in the subsequent figure. This alignment preserves the original symmetric distribution of weights and greatly enhances model performance.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F7" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2408.08554v3/QQ_o.png" id="A1.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:684/407;" width="684" height="407" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>Quantile-Quantile Plots of data distribution with o_proj weights in the 1st, 10th, 20th, and 30th blocks at full precision (up), INT2 quantization (middle) and INT2* quantization (below) in the LLaMA-7B model</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Arbitrary Bit Matrix Calculation</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Formally, given a p-bit weight matrix W and a q-bit activation matrix X, we can first decompose into 1-bit matrices <math id="A2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{s},\quad s\in\left\{0,1,...,p-1\right\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>s</mi></msup><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{s},\quad s\in\left\{0,1,...,p-1\right\}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X^{t},\quad t\in\left\{0,1,...,p-1\right\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X^{t},\quad t\in\left\{0,1,...,p-1\right\}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
<table id="A2.E8" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="A2.E8X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A2.E8X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle w^{s}_{i,j}=\left(w_{i,j}\gg s\right)\&amp;1,\quad x^{t}_{i,j}=\left(x_{i,j}\gg t\right)\&amp;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>s</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≫</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">&amp;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≫</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">&amp;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle w^{s}_{i,j}=\left(w_{i,j}\gg s\right)\&amp;1,\quad x^{t}_{i,j}=\left(x_{i,j}\gg t\right)\&amp;1</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">If BMMA stands for 1-bit matrix multiplication, then the BMMA operation can be called <math id="A2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\times q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\times q</annotation></semantics></math> times to compute a series of 1-bit matrix multiplication components</p>
<table id="A2.E9" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="A2.E9X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A2.E9X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle Y^{s,t}=BMMA\left(W^{s},X^{t}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>s</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle Y^{s,t}=BMMA\left(W^{s},X^{t}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p1.4" class="ltx_p">Finally, we process all 1-bit matrix multiplication components with bit-stacked scaling factors, after which they are summed to obtain a 32-bit output matrix</p>
<table id="A2.E10" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="A2.E10X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A2.E10X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle Y=\sum_{s=0}^{p-1}\sum_{t=0}^{q-1}Y^{s,t}\ast 2^{s+t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover></mstyle><msup><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle Y=\sum_{s=0}^{p-1}\sum_{t=0}^{q-1}Y^{s,t}\ast 2^{s+t}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p1.5" class="ltx_p">After the above transformation process, we decompose the operation of arbitrary quantized combinations into a special superposition of 1-bit matrix multiplications, so that the underlying layer can be implemented by calling high-computing BMMA instructions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Full Results for Quantization Algorithms</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we mainly publish metrics for per-channel/per-token quantization. However, ABQ-LLM is naturally orthogonal to per-group quantization, and we validate this on LLaMA-7B for W4A4 g128 per-group quantization with the results shown in Table <a href="#A3.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Appendix C Full Results for Quantization Algorithms ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>. Experimental results demonstrate that, in most cases, our method outperforms another state-of-the-art (SOTA) method, Atom<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al. 2024</a>)</cite>, which employs per-group quantization. Additionally, our method exhibits a degradation of less than 0.5 in PPL compared to FP16, indicating excellent performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, we present the perplexity (PPL) metrics and zero-shot performance of ABQ-LLM under various quantization configurations. Unfortunately, most prior work has not disclosed complete experimental data, with only PPL metrics for common configurations such as W4A16, W3A16, W2A16, W4A4, and W6A6 being published. Additionally, the full zero-shot results were not made publicly available. We aim to establish a comprehensive quantization baseline for post-training quantization (PTQ) by making our extensive data publicly accessible. However, due to limitations in time and computational resources, we can only provide our own comprehensive experimental results and cannot fully reproduce the results of other baselines.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.T5" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A3.T5.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="A3.T5.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A3.T5.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" rowspan="2"><span id="A3.T5.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text">Bits</span></th>
<th id="A3.T5.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" rowspan="2"><span id="A3.T5.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text">Method</span></th>
<th id="A3.T5.1.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" colspan="2">PPL<math id="A3.T5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math></th>
<th id="A3.T5.1.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" colspan="7">Accuracy(%)<math id="A3.T5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math></th></tr>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>Performance of weight-activation per-group quantization on LLaMA-7B with a group size of 128.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure the reproducibility of our results, we specify that for the PPL test, we follow the GPTQ method by setting the sentence length to 2048. It is important to note that different sentence lengths may affect the accuracy of the metrics. Additionally, for the zero-shot accuracy test, two metrics may be used: <span id="A3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">acc</span> or <span id="A3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">acc_norm</span>. If <span id="A3.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">acc_norm</span> is available, we report <span id="A3.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">acc_norm</span>; otherwise, we report the <span id="A3.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">acc</span> metric. Finally, we have published the quantized model series on the Huggingface platform. Table <a href="#A3.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Appendix C Full Results for Quantization Algorithms ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> presents the perplexity metrics for weight-only quantization, while Table <a href="#A3.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Appendix C Full Results for Quantization Algorithms ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> displays the perplexity metrics for various configurations where both weights and activations are quantized simultaneously. The zero-shot accuracies of LLaMA-7B, LLaMA-13B, LLaMA-2-7B, and LLaMA-2-13B are shown in Tables <a href="#A3.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ Appendix C Full Results for Quantization Algorithms ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>, <a href="#A3.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ Appendix C Full Results for Quantization Algorithms ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, <a href="#A3.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ Appendix C Full Results for Quantization Algorithms ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, and <a href="#A3.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ Appendix C Full Results for Quantization Algorithms ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>, respectively. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms other baselines across all quantization configurations, achieving state-of-the-art performance in both weight-only quantization and weight-activation quantization.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>GPU Kernel Optimization Details</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GEMV Elimination.</span> Our custom engine decomposes the operation of arbitrary quantized combinations into a superposition of 1-bit matrix multiplications. As for GEMV problems, multiple single-bit GEMV are converted to GEMM, fully utilizing the TensorCore while reducing or even avoiding the redundant computation caused by padding. For the <math id="A4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{q}A_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{q}A_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> configuration, the actual computing task undertaken by ABQKernel is p*M × q*N × K. When p*M % MMA_M = 0, we can achieve zero redundant calculation. As shown in Figure <a href="#A4.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Appendix D GPU Kernel Optimization Details ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, there are two problems with directly calling INT8 TensorCore to execute W2A8 GEMV: 1. Converting W2 to W8 online requires additional instructions. 2. When M <math id="A4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>=</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=</annotation></semantics></math> 1 and MMA_M <math id="A4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>=</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=</annotation></semantics></math> 8, calling TensorCore will introduce 87.5% redundant calculations. In contrast, ABQKernel achieves direct acceleration of W2A8 without any redundant computation.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.F8" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2408.08554v3/gemv_row.drawio.png" id="A4.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:698/188;" width="698" height="188" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>Overview of GEMV Elimination. </figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Computational Pipeline Optimization.</span> Figure <a href="#A4.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ Appendix D GPU Kernel Optimization Details ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> illustrates our optimization of the computation pipeline to enhance inference performance within the widely adopted Ampere architecture. At the shared memory level, we perform asynchronous writes from global memory to shared memory using the <span id="A4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">cp.async</span> instruction to hide the latency of subsequent memory accesses. Before processing the first loop, a synchronization instruction ensures that TILE-0, the data required by the first loop, has been written to shared memory. During the processing of the first loop, TILE-1, the data needed for the second loop, is asynchronously written to shared memory. This concurrent execution of data writes for the second loop and computation of the first loop masks the shared memory access latency for subsequent loops. For register-level optimization within the loop, when k=0, TILE-0 data from shared memory is loaded into the first set of registers <span id="A4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A0</span> and <span id="A4.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">B0</span>, while the data required for k=1 is preloaded into registers <span id="A4.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A1</span> and <span id="A4.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">B1</span>. Once the data in registers <span id="A4.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A0</span> and <span id="A4.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">B0</span> is ready, the bmma operation is performed on <span id="A4.p2.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A0</span> and <span id="A4.p2.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">B0</span>. When k=1, the data <span id="A4.p2.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A1</span> and <span id="A4.p2.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">B1</span> needed for bmma has already been preloaded at k=0, and the data required for k=2 is preloaded into registers <span id="A4.p2.1.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A0</span> and <span id="A4.p2.1.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">B0</span>, and so on. By doubling the register cache, data is written from shared memory to registers during the Tensor Core bmma computation, effectively masking the register access time. Where bmma denotes a 1-bit matrix multiplication operation, while TILE data refers to a block of data obtained after partitioning and processing the original dataset.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.F9" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2408.08554v3/pipeline.png" id="A4.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:698/240;" width="698" height="240" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span>Space-time diagram of the computational pipeline.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Auto Kernel Search.</span> To utilize GPU memory more efficiently at all levels, a chunking strategy is essential during computation. Chunk size is crucial for GEMM performance. Before launching an arbitrary precision inference operator, we perform performance tests on different chunk sizes to select the best implementation. As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.2 Improving Quantization by Distribution Correction ‣ 3 Method ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, for the classical GEMM task, the M × N × K problem is usually chunked by BM × BN × BK at the thread block level, and each thread block is chunked by WM × WN × WK at the warp level. Each warp gets MMA_M × MMA_N × MMA_K based on the Tensor Core chunk size supported by the GPU model and searches for different chunk shapes after obtaining the chunk sizes at the three levels. In the arbitrary precision operator, the number of weight bits (q) and activation bits (p) also need to be considered, so the search space is larger compared to the classical GEMM. Given the BTC chunk sizes MMA_M = 8, MMA_N = 8, MMA_K = 128, the number of weighted warps is computed as W_WARPS_NUM = BN × q / WN, and the number of activation warps is computed as X_WARPS_NUM = BM × p / WM. The total number of warps is 1 <math id="A4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≤</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq</annotation></semantics></math> X_WARPS_NUM × W_WARPS_NUM <math id="A4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≤</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq</annotation></semantics></math> 32. To reduce the search space, we fix WK = MMA_K = 128 and set the length of BK to 128, 256, 384, 512. BM, BN, BK, WM, and WN cannot be infinitely large due to the limited shared memory and register usage of a single thread block. As for <math id="A4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{q}A_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{q}A_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> configuration, the design process of a candidate instance in the search space is summarized as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">1. Determine the number and layout of Warps contained in the Thread Block based on expert experience. for example, X_WARPS_NUM × W_WARPS_NUM = 1 × 4.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">2. Determine the Thread Block Tile(<math id="A4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math>BM, BN, BK<math id="A4.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math>) with the smallest redundant padding based on the quantized bit width p of the activation and the M dimension of the computing task.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">3. The size of the WARP Tile(<math id="A4.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math>WM, WN, WK<math id="A4.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math>) is calculated based on the layout of Warps and Thread Block Tile. Ultimately, we test the operators at various chunk sizes and adopt the speed-optimized implementation.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.F10" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2408.08554v3/noswizing.png" id="A4.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:698/236;" width="698" height="236" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 10: </span>Address occurs shared memory 4-way bank conflicts. E denotes an <span id="A4.F10.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">e</span>lement of int32, B denotes <span id="A4.F10.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">b</span>ank, and T denotes a <span id="A4.F10.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">t</span>hread.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A4.F11" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2408.08554v3/swizing.png" id="A4.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:698/235;" width="698" height="235" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 11: </span>Address remapping avoids shared memory bank conflicts. E denotes an element of int32, B denotes bank, and T denotes
a thread.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A4.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bank Conflicts Elimination.</span> For attaining high bandwidth, shared memory is segmented into memory modules of uniform size, which are referred to as banks. Each bank occupies 4 bytes, and the continuous 128 bytes in the shared memory form 32 banks. Threads within a warp can access data from various banks simultaneously in one single memory access request. However, if multiple threads access data within the same bank concurrently, it will give rise to a bank conflict, leading to lower throughput.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p8.1" class="ltx_p">The above Figure <a href="#A4.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ Appendix D GPU Kernel Optimization Details ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> shows the scenario where bank conflict occurs (BM=8, BK=512), where E denotes an <span id="A4.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">e</span>lement of int32, B denotes <span id="A4.p8.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">b</span>ank, and T denotes a <span id="A4.p8.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">t</span>hread. When data is loaded from global memory to shared memory, each thread accesses 16 bytes in order to fully utilize the memory bandwidth. The 8x512-bit data is divided into four phases, each reading 128 bytes (i.e., two consecutive rows of data in the figure). During this process, no Bank conflicts occur in any of the phases.
However, when data is loaded from shared memory to registers, each thread needs to copy 4 bytes of data since the 8x8x128 BMMA stores matrix A (8x128 bits) and matrix B (8x128 bits) in 32-bit registers. When copying a matrix block (same color block), threads T0˜3, T8˜11, T16˜19, and T24˜27 all access B0˜3, while T4˜7, T12˜15, T20˜23, and T28˜31 access B16˜19, resulting in 4-way bank conflicts.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p9.1" class="ltx_p">As depicted in the Figure <a href="#A4.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ Appendix D GPU Kernel Optimization Details ‣ ABQ-LLM: Arbitrary-Bit Quantized Inference Acceleration for Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>, we employ the swizzle operation to address this issue. When the global memory is loaded into the shared memory, the addresses are swizzled, causing the 8x128bit data to be scattered across 32 banks. When T0˜31 accesses 8x128bit data, the data comes from B0˜31 respectively, and no bank conflict will arise, thereby further improving the efficiency of memory access.</p>
</div>

    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
  </div>
